state.misconception_label: Does not know the properties of a rectangle

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The angles highlighted on this rectangle with different length sides can never be... ![A rectangle with the diagonals drawn in. The angle on the right hand side at the centre is highlighted in red and the angle at the bottom at the centre is highlighted in yellow.](). I got acute because I assumed all the angles in the figure are equal.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Imagine you are building a house with rectangular rooms. The intersecting diagonals of a rectangle are like the walls meeting at a corner. Just like how the walls create right angles, the diagonals in a rectangle also create right angles. So, the angles highlighted in the rectangle with different length sides can never be acute because they must always be right angles.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Oh, I see what you mean about the walls and right angles! So, the angles where the diagonals meet are always right angles, right? But what about the other angles in the rectangle? Are they all right angles too?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Think about a rhombus, where all four sides are equal in length. Just like how all the sides of a rhombus are equal, in a rectangle, opposite sides are equal in length. So, the angles in a rectangle that are not at the intersection of the diagonals will also be right angles because of this property.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Okay, I think I get it! So all the angles in a rectangle are right angles, not just the ones where the diagonals meet. But what about rectangles that are not squares? Do they still have right angles even if the sides are different lengths?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher provides mathematically incorrect information (diagonals of rectangles do not create right angles at their intersection unless it's a square), simply tells rather than prompts reasoning, and the student remains confused about basic rectangle properties by the end.
score.justification_pass2: While Turn 1 attempts an experiential approach with the house-building analogy, Turn 3 abandons this strategy entirely by introducing abstract geometric properties of rhombuses without any real-world connection, and the analogy in Turn 1 is also mathematically incorrect (diagonals of rectangles don't generally create right angles).
